title: The Gopis Search the Forest
story:
One moment he was there among them; the next, the gopis turned and he was gone. No word, no warning — only the empty place where Krishna had stood.

They did not go home. They went into the forest, the way the verses say it: like women out of their minds, searching from wood to wood and singing his name aloud so that all of Vrindavan could hear it. The moonlight fell in pieces through the leaves, and still they went on, their bare feet finding the paths between the trees, their voices lifting and falling in the dark.

And as they searched, they began to take on his very manner. The verses say his walk, his smile, the way he glanced, the sweet way he spoke — all of it rose up in them as they went, until each gopi seemed to carry a little of him in her own step and voice. To see them was to see him, scattered among a hundred women.

And because they had no one else to ask, they questioned the trees. They stopped before the ashvattha and the plaksha and the great banyan, the holy fig trees of the forest, and asked: have you seen Nanda's son? They turned to the flowering trees — the ashoka, the kurabaka, the champaka, the nagakesara and the punnaga — and to the tulasi plant, which they called the one beloved of Govinda's feet, and put the same question to each of them. Have you seen him, the one who stole our hearts with his smiles?

They asked the mango and the jackfruit and the kadamba, the bilva and the bakula and the nipa, the jasmine and the creepers that twine up the trunks of the forest trees, the creepers the verses picture throwing their arms around a great tree like a friend embracing a friend. They even turned on the earth itself and demanded to know what penance it had performed, that the mere touch of his feet should make it blossom the way it did — whether it was his stride or the touch of his feet that had set the whole ground breaking into flowers. And they asked the doe, wondering whether Krishna had come this way — his arm resting on a beloved's shoulder, a lotus in his hand, the garland of tulasi around his neck and the bees following him, drunk on its scent, the jasmine garland carrying a faint perfume of the one he loved — and whether the trees had bowed to him as he passed, honored by one long, loving glance.

But the forest kept its silence. The trees held their branches still. The gopis went on from tree to tree, calling the question again and again, because asking was the only thing left to do.

They were not looking for news of him. They were looking for him. And somewhere in the middle of it the search stopped being a search for a lost person and became the only way they knew to keep him near — to keep saying his name, to keep his walk and his smile before their eyes, even when he would not show himself.
reflection: The gopis address trees and creepers as if they could answer, which is the whole heart of the passage: when the beloved vanishes, love turns the whole world into a possible messenger. Their grief does not sit still; it moves, questions, and fills the forest with his name.
next_story_tease: And when the trees gave no answer, their searching turned to something stranger still.
hero_scene: The gopis wandering the moonlit Vrindavan forest, singing Krishna's name aloud and stopping before the great fig and flowering trees to ask, Have you seen Nanda's son?
